notes.h: Who the unionists were and why they opposed Home Rule
notes.b: Unionism united Ulster Protestants of all classes with southern landlords and business interests, who feared Home Rule for religious, economic and imperial reasons.
points: Unionists were mainly Protestants, especially in east Ulster, but the movement also drew on southern landlords, business people and the Church of Ireland.
Religious opposition rested on the belief that a Dublin parliament would be dominated by the Catholic majority, and the slogan Home Rule is Rome Rule summed up this fear.
Economic opposition was strongest in Belfast, where the linen, shipbuilding and engineering industries depended on the imperial market and on protection from Home Rule taxation.
Identity and empire: unionists saw themselves as British, and they regarded Home Rule as a step towards separation from the United Kingdom.
Southern unionists, including many landlords, were concentrated in Dublin and the Munster and Leinster counties, and they were a minority among Protestants in the south.

notes.h: Organisation: the Orange Order and the unionist bodies (1885–1905)
notes.b: Unionist opposition took organised form in the 1880s and 1890s, and the Ulster Unionist Council of 1905 gave Ulster a central body.
points: The Orange Order revived in the 1880s and expanded its membership and its lodges in Ulster as a focus of Protestant loyalty.
The Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union was founded in 1885 to co-ordinate opposition to Home Rule across Ireland.
The Ulster Convention of June 1892 in Belfast protested against Gladstone’s second Home Rule Bill and showed the strength of unionist mobilisation.
The Ulster Unionist Council was set up in 1905 as a central body for Ulster unionism, bringing together representatives from the province’s counties and boroughs.
James Craig, a Belfast businessman and MP, worked closely with Carson in organising the unionist campaign, and became Carson’s chief organiser.

notes.b: Carson, a Dublin-born lawyer, made himself the leader of Ulster unionism and organised armed resistance to Home Rule.
points: Edward Carson (1854–1935) was born in Dublin, trained as a barrister, and served as Solicitor General for Ireland from 1892 to 1893.
Carson prosecuted Oscar Wilde in 1895, a case that increased his public profile in England.
Carson became leader of the Irish Unionist parliamentary party in 1910, after Walter Long, and he was the principal figure of unionist resistance from then until 1914.
As a participant, Carson led the Ulster Day rally in Belfast on 28 September 1912 and signed the Solemn League and Covenant in the same week.
Carson was not a bystander to the Home Rule crisis: he shaped unionist strategy in the Commons and in the Ulster campaign, and he led the resistance from Belfast.
Contemporary unionists admired him as the defender of the Union, while nationalists and some Liberals saw him as a leader prepared to use armed resistance to block a democratic decision.

Historians differ: some judge him a determined defender of Protestant rights who forced the government to exclude Ulster, others a leader whose threat of force helped to make the partition settlement of 1914 possible.

Carson’s achievements were the mobilisation of the Ulster Volunteers and the exclusion proposals; his limits were that the exclusion of Ulster was never fully agreed and that Irish unionists did not win the Union.

notes.h: The Conservative alliance and the Solemn League and Covenant (1912)
notes.b: The Conservatives gave unionism parliamentary support in 1912, and the Covenant mobilised Protestant opposition on a mass scale.
points: Bonar Law, the Conservative leader, spoke at a rally at Blenheim Palace in July 1912, and his speech committed the party to support the unionist resistance.
The Solemn League and Covenant was signed on 28 September 1912, with the great majority of signatures collected in Ulster, the total being about 470,000 (about, verify).
Men who signed the Covenant pledged to resist Home Rule by all means necessary, and the document was the foundation of the Ulster Volunteer Force.
Women signed a separate covenant, and the campaign gave unionist women a public role in the resistance.

notes.h: The Ulster Volunteer Force and the gun-running (1913–1914)
notes.b: Unionists formed an armed force in 1913 and imported rifles in 1914, which led to the Curragh incident.
points: The Ulster Volunteer Force was formed in January 1913 to resist Home Rule by force, with Carson as its leader and Craig as its organiser.
The UVF drilled openly in Ulster from 1913 onwards, and its membership rose into the tens of thousands.
The Larne gun-running, in April 1914, landed about 25,000 rifles and millions of rounds of ammunition at Larne, Co. Antrim, under the organisation of Fred Crawford (about).
The Curragh incident of March 1914 was a crisis in which British army officers at the Curragh camp, Co. Kildare, indicated they would resign rather than move against Ulster.
The incident was seen by nationalists as proof that the army would not enforce Home Rule against Ulster, and by unionists as a sign of the government’s weakness.

notes.h: The exclusion question and the Buckingham Palace Conference (1914)
notes.b: The problem of Ulster was debated at Westminster and at the Buckingham Palace Conference in July 1914, which failed to agree a settlement.
points: Carson demanded the exclusion of all nine Ulster counties, and later the six counties of north-east Ulster, from any Home Rule arrangement.
Redmond opposed the permanent exclusion of Ulster, and he proposed a temporary exclusion, which Carson and the unionists rejected.
The Buckingham Palace Conference, held in July 1914 under the king’s chairmanship, brought together the party leaders to settle the Ulster question, but it failed to reach agreement.
The outbreak of war in August 1914 suspended the Home Rule Act and postponed the question of Ulster’s exclusion until after the war.

notes.b: Judgements on unionism compare its success in blocking Home Rule before 1914 with its failure to prevent Irish independence.
points: Achievement: by 1914 unionists had forced the government to accept the principle of exclusion for part of Ulster and had shown that armed resistance could delay Home Rule.
Limit: unionist resistance could not prevent the Home Rule Act from passing, and the Union with Ireland was not secured in the long term.
Contemporary nationalists judged unionist arms as a threat to democracy, while unionists judged them a legitimate defence of the Union and of Protestant rights.
Later historians differ on how far the Ulster crisis made partition inevitable, and some see it as the first step towards the settlement of 1920–21.

keyTerms.definition: The movement opposed to Home Rule, which wanted Ireland to remain part of the United Kingdom with Westminster legislation for the whole country.
The use of armed volunteer forces as a political instrument, which the Ulster Volunteer Force used in 1913–14 to resist Home Rule.
The unionist slogan that Home Rule would bring Catholic domination of an Irish parliament and of Protestant interests.
The body set up in 1905 to co-ordinate unionist opposition to Home Rule in Ulster, which chose Carson as its leader in 1910.
The declaration signed on 28 September 1912 by Ulster unionists pledging resistance to Home Rule.
The armed unionist force formed in January 1913 to resist Home Rule by force if necessary.
The April 1914 landing of rifles and ammunition at Larne, Co. Antrim, for the Ulster Volunteers.
The March 1914 crisis in which British army officers at the Curragh indicated they would resign rather than move against Ulster.
